g.passage: Conrad Dasipodius was a man for whom the simplest objects of daily life had borne a significance. It had been his nature to see “sermons in stones, and good in everything”; and could he have looked on this scene before him, with all its wedded glory of nature and of art, he must have found in it some anodyne for the gnawing pain of hope disappointed. But he could have no part now in such joys, and to him the world was a dull leaden-hued wilderness. Winter and summer, day and night, in all the years to come, the same. A dismal chaos, a dark and thorny way indeed, where love and friendship had left him in his utmost need, to blunder on alone.
g.question: Which choice best describes how the tone of the text shifts?
options: From mild amusement to quiet pride in Conrad's achievements
From harsh criticism to gentle forgiveness of Conrad's faults
From restless anticipation to calm contentment with the scene
From appreciation of Conrad's outlook to bleak desolation
g.explanation: 처음에는 일상의 사물에서도 의미를 찾던 Conrad의 기질을 긍정적으로 묘사한다. 그러나 'But he could have no part now in such joys' 이후 세상이 '납빛 황무지'가 되었다는 절망적 어조로 바뀌므로 D가 정답이다. A와 C는 후반의 어두운 분위기와 맞지 않는다. B는 Conrad를 비판하는 부분이 없어 틀리다.

g.passage:
The girl, tall and strong, walking with the ease that comes from health and a steadfast mind; the eager, restless boy running and jumping by her side. Barebone must have seen them as soon as they saw him. They were part of Farlingford, these two. He had a sudden feeling of having been away for years, with this difference--that he came back and found nothing changed. Whereas, in reality, he who returns after a long absence usually finds no one awaiting him.

He did as Sep had foretold--crossing to the far side of the river, and then gaining the mouth of the creek in one tack.

options: It describes two figures, gives Barebone's reflection on returning, then shows him sailing.
It recounts a quarrel between two figures, then explains why Barebone left the town.
It praises Farlingford's landscape, then lists the changes Barebone finds on his return.
It presents Sep's warning about the river, then describes the girl's response to it.
g.explanation: 지문은 먼저 소녀와 소년의 모습을 묘사하고, 이어 Barebone이 오랜 부재 후 아무것도 변하지 않았다고 느끼는 생각을 제시한 뒤, 마지막에 그가 강을 건너 배를 모는 행동으로 넘어간다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B의 다툼, C의 변화 목록은 지문에 없다. D는 Sep의 예언이 마지막에 짧게 언급될 뿐 글의 출발점이 아니므로 틀리다.

g.passage: The dawn was breaking, and at its first sign the escort of Saladin’s soldiers had turned and left them, saying that now they were safe in their own country. All night they had ridden fast and far. The plain was behind them, and their road ran among hills. Suddenly it turned, and in the flaming lights of the new-born day showed them a sight so beautiful that for a moment all that little company drew rein to gaze. For yonder before them, though far away as yet, throned upon her hills, stood the holy city of Jerusalem.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It explains why the escort left, then describes a battle with Saladin's soldiers.
It recounts a night's journey into the hills, then reveals a striking view of Jerusalem.
It describes Jerusalem in detail, then recalls the hardships of reaching the city.
It contrasts the plain with the hills, then explains why the company turned back.
g.explanation: 지문은 호위대가 떠나고 밤새 달려 언덕길에 들어선 여정을 먼저 서술한다. 이어 길이 꺾이며 새벽빛 속에 예루살렘이 나타나는 장면으로 마무리되므로 B가 정답이다. A의 전투, D의 회군은 지문에 없다. C는 순서가 반대이며 도시를 자세히 묘사하지도 않는다.

g.passage: At the supper-table he talked much and well, exceedingly well, I thought, except when he touched on the war, which he was continually doing, and then I was on tenter-hooks. His point of view was so opposed to ours as to threaten in several instances to bring on an engagement all along the line. This calamity was averted by my passing something to him at the critical moment. Now I checked his advance by a slice of cold tongue, and now I turned his flank with another cup of tea; but I questioned my ability to preserve peace throughout the evening. Before the meal was at an end there had crept into Clara's manner a polite calmness which I never liked to see.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward the supper conversation?
options: Bored indifference to the guest's lengthy remarks about the war
Open hostility toward the guest's opinions about the war
Delighted admiration for Clara's skill in calming the guest
Anxious but wry watchfulness over a dispute about to erupt
g.explanation: 화자는 손님이 전쟁 이야기를 할 때마다 '바늘방석'에 앉은 듯했다고 말한다. 또 혀 요리와 차 한 잔으로 그의 '진격을 막고 측면을 돌렸다'고 전쟁 비유를 써 자신의 노력을 익살스럽게 묘사하므로 D가 정답이다. A는 화자가 대화를 잘 들었다고 칭찬해 틀리다. B는 화자가 오히려 평화를 지키려 하고, C는 Clara가 차갑게 변한 것을 싫어하므로 틀리다.

g.passage:
There was no time to protest or to ask questions. And Juliette felt herself passed on from one pair of strong arms to another, until she was standing on the deck under the humming rigging, surrounded by men who seemed huge in their gleaming oil-skins.

"This way, mademoiselle," said one, who was even larger than the others, in English, of which she understood enough to catch his meaning. "I will take you to your father. Show a light this way, one of you."

His fingers closed round her arm, and he led her, unconscious of a strength that almost lifted her from her feet, toward an open door, where a lamp burnt dimly within.
g.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Juliette argues with the sailors before agreeing to board.
Juliette struggles to understand the sailors' foreign speech.
Juliette is brought aboard and led toward her father.
Juliette searches the deck alone for a lamp and a door.
g.explanation: Juliette는 질문할 틈도 없이 여러 팔에 넘겨져 갑판에 서게 되고, 가장 큰 선원이 아버지에게 데려가겠다며 그녀를 문 쪽으로 이끈다. 이 두 장면을 합치면 C가 요지이다. A는 '항의할 시간이 없었다'는 서술과 어긋난다. B는 그녀가 뜻을 이해했다고 하므로 틀리고, D는 그녀가 혼자가 아니라 이끌려 간다.

g.passage: I bent my head, and seemed to receive the Atlantic on my back. The world seemed going to destruction. I could not see anything, the flood poured down savagely. I raised my head, with open mouth, and the most of the American cataract went down my throat. If I had sprung a leak now I had been lost. And at this moment I discovered that the bridge had ceased, and we must trust for a foothold to the slippery and precipitous rocks. I never was so scared before and survived it. But we got through at last, and emerged into the open day, where we could stand in front of the laced and frothy and seething world of descending water, and look at it.

g.passage: I slipped through one of these cracks, went up a swept and ungarnished staircase, as arid as a desert, and opened the first door I came to. Two women, one fat and the other slim, sat on straw-bottomed chairs, knitting black wool. The slim one got up and walked straight at me—still knitting with downcast eyes—and only just as I began to think of getting out of her way, as you would for a somnambulist, stood still, and looked up. Her dress was as plain as an umbrella-cover, and she turned round without a word and preceded me into a waiting-room. I gave my name, and looked about. Deal table in the middle, plain chairs all round the walls, on one end a large shining map, marked with all the colours of a rainbow.

options: a place made dangerous by heat and dust
a space that is bare and without warmth

g.explanation: 구절 바로 앞의 'swept and ungarnished'는 계단이 깨끗이 쓸렸지만 아무 장식도 없음을 보여 준다. 이어지는 평범한 의자, 우산 덮개 같은 옷차림 묘사도 삭막한 분위기를 이어 가므로 B가 정답이다. A와 C는 사막을 문자 그대로 받아들인 해석이다. D는 계단의 경사나 길이에 대한 언급이 없어 틀리다.

g.passage: One last word about our amiable author. His great book remains eminently alive, and wields after two centuries and a half a permanent influence. When you refer to it, you must not expect a logical development of philosophical theory. We do not look to find a system in a book of maxims and portraits. La Bruyere was a moralist, pure and simple; he awakened sensibility, he encouraged refinement, and he exposed the vicious difference which existed around him--and which no one else had seemed to notice--that the possession of more or fewer pieces of money made between human beings otherwise equal.

options: is filled with vivid scenes of physical action

g.passage: I took off its hat and cloak to see if there were any strings cutting its neck or choking it. Then I glanced at the feet, and lo! there was the trouble. The boots were at least one size too small. I took them off, and the stockings, too, and found the feet as cold as ice and the prints of the stockings clearly traced on the tender flesh. We all know the agony of tight boots. I rubbed the feet and held them in my hands until they were warm, when the poor little thing fell asleep.
